NCBN Thermal Report

June 02, 2026

Background

Eelgrass Importance and Vulnerability

Eelgrass (Zostera marina) is a foundational marine plant that supports healthy coastal ecosystems. It improves water quality, stabilizes sediments, provides habitat for fish and invertebrates, and acts as a globally important carbon sink (Novak et al. 2023).Because eelgrass responds quickly to changes in its environment, it is often considered a “canary in the coal mine” for coastal health (Orth et al. 2006). Its ecological significance is one reason the Northeast Coastal and Barrier Network (NCBN) monitors seagrass conditions over time, especially as concerns rise about the effects of warming waters.

In recent decades, eelgrass along the Northeast U.S. coast has experienced water temperatures that approach or exceed known physiological limits (Nagel et. al 2025a,b,c). When water becomes too warm, eelgrass respiration increases faster than photosynthesis, creating stress on the plants. Studies show that temperatures above 25 °C increase the likelihood of eelgrass mortality, and sustained exposure above 30 °C has led to complete die offs in areas such as Chesapeake Bay (Jarvis & Moore 2010, Novak et al. 2023). Long term temperature records from New Hampshire to Maryland indicate that warmer summers are consistently followed by lower eelgrass presence in the next year (Plaisted et al. 2022). When high temperature events persist without cooling relief periods, eelgrass loses the opportunity to recover from heat stress. Repeated summers with limited relief causes stress to accumulate and increases the risk of widespread decline.

These patterns of warmer summers, increased physiological stress, and fewer opportunities for recovery align with broader climate driven trends. Marine heatwaves, periods when water temperatures exceed the 90th percentile of a 30 year baseline, have become more frequent and more intense (Hobday etl al 2016). Such events have already affected corals, kelp forests, and seagrasses worldwide. Research shows that eelgrass meadows experiencing both high heat and little cooling tend to lose shoot density and canopy height, while sites that receive periodic cooling are better able to recover between heat events (Berger et al. 2024).

Other marine systems use cumulative heat stress metrics to understand ecosystem and species lvel impacts. NOAA’s Degree Heating Weeks (DHW) index, for example, tracks how much and how long temperatures exceed thresholds that lead to coral bleaching and mortality (Skirving et al. 2020). These tools emphasize that it is the accumulation of heat over time, not single temperature spikes, that often drive ecosystem decline. This same concept is directly relevant to eelgrass.

Calculating cumulative stress frameworks requires long term temperature datasets. To better understand how warming affects eelgrass within the Northeast Coastal and Barrier Network parks, we used long term temperature datasets to:

  1. Identify years with extreme heat and limited cooling,
  2. Determine where these conditions overlapped to create compounded “stress years,” and
  3. Compare patterns across parks to understand regional vulnerability.

Methods

Protocol

The Northeast Coastal and Barrier Network uses the Tier-3 standardized Estuarine Nutrient Enrichment monitoring protocol (Kopp and Neckles, 2009) that includes seagrass condition monitoring (SOP 9). Seagrass condition is assessed using measures of population and shoot structure to track changes in meadow condition over time. The protocol was adapted from the international SeagrassNet program, which provides standardized methods for monitoring seagrass ecosystems.

Within the network, three coastal parks, Assateague Island National Seashore (ASIS), Cape Cod National Seashore, and Fire Island National Seashore (FIIS) implement the Tier-3 seagrass monitoring protocol. At ASIS, long-term seagrass condition is monitored at one site: Tingles Island.

At each long-term monitoring site, seagrass condition is monitored across three permanent 50-m transects that run parallel to shore at a shallow, mid-depth, and deep depth. Temperature loggers (HOBO UTBI-001 Tidbit Temp, Onset Computer Corporation) are attached to each transect and record water temperature at continuous 15-minute intervals throughout the year.

Following data collection, water temperature data from each year are uploaded to the NPS AQUARIUS WebPortal for QAQC, certification, and storage. Additional details about data collection at each site are shown in Table 1 below.

Data Summerization & Analysis

For this analysis, we focused on the continuous water temperature data and examined patterns of thermal stress and cooling dynamics with the goals of understanding the thermal conditions at ASIS and comparing with those at other long-term monitoring sites at CACO and FIIS.

Prior to analyses, temperature data were first filtered to the months from May-September to hone in on when thermal stress likely occurs. To ensure that the data from each sampling year occurred consistently over the same time periods, we then further filtered the data from each site to only include years with 80% data coverage and with at least 10 days of data in a minimum of three of the five focal months. Then, data from the individual transects at each site were summarized up to a single thermal metric value (HDH or CDH) for each year as described in the next section.

Novel Thermal Metrics for Eelgrass

For eelgrass, prolonged exposure to high temperatures can lead to physiological stress where respiration outpaces photosynthesis. To describe long-term thermal conditions in eelgrass meadows, we calculated two site-level yearly metrics from the continuous water temperature data: heating degree hours (HDH) and cooling degree hours (CDH) (Berger et al. 2024). HDH is calculated by first summing the total number of hours above a park-specific temperature threshold across the focal months (May to September) to get the total HDH per year. The total HDH values are then divided by the sum of all hours in the period of record for each year to get the mean HDH per year. Similarly, mean CDH for each year is calculated using the same method but for the number of hours below the site-specific temperature threshold. We applied a threshold of 25 °C for northern sites (CACO and FIIS) and 28.6 °C for southern sites (ASIS) (Berger and Berg 2024) based on known values of eelgrass thermal tolerance reported in peer-reviewed literature. Thus, these metrics capture not just how hot or cold the water gets, but how long water temperatures remain above or below a biological threshold. When examined together, HDH and CDH help to understand the factors controlling eelgrass loss and recovery across coastal National Parks in the northeast (Figure 1).

Figure 1. Conceptualized diagrams demonstrating how yearly heating degree hours (HDH) and cooling degree hours (CDH) are calculated for each site.

Site-Specific Extremes

Within each site at ASIS, we identified extreme high heat years as those years where the mean HDH was above the site-specific 90th percentile (28.5°C). These years represent years when the eelgrass meadow at these sites experienced the most intense and prolonged thermal stress. Similarly, we also identified extreme low cooling years as those years where the mean CDH was above the 90th percentile for each site. In this context, lower CDH values (i.e., more negative) represent greater cooling below the temperature threshold at each site, indicating potential periods of relief for eelgrass meadows. Finally, we identified compound stress years as those years with both extreme high heat and extreme low cooling.

Regional Comparisons

In order to understand regional patterns of seagrass thermal stress and cooling relief among coastal parks in the northeast, we used k-means cluster analysis to categorize each site in ASIS, CACO, and FIIS into four thermal stress regimes and four cooling relief regimes. K-means cluster analyses were conducted using 4 centers (to represent the 4 thermal stress or cooling relief regimes) and 2 random sets via the algorithm defined by Hartigan and Wong as implemented in the ‘kmeans’ function from the ‘stats’ package in R.

The four thermal stress regimes were based on 1) the % time above the previously mentioned park-specific threshold averaged across all years (i.e., duration of warming), and 2) the number of warming events averaged across all years (i.e., frequency of warming). Thermal stress regimes were defined as:

  • Episodic Heatwave: Sites with infrequent, but intense heat events
  • Highly Stressed: Sites with frequent and prolonged heat events
  • Low Exposure: Sites with infrequent and limited time above thermal threshold
  • Chronic Warming: Sites with frequent heat events that are not prolonged (pulsing)

The four cooling relief regimes were based on 1) the mean cooling degree hours averaged across all years at each site, and 2) the mean heating degree hours averaged across all years at each site. Cooling relief regimes were defined as:

  • Stable Systems: Low heat stress and moderate cooling
  • Chronic Heat Stress: High heat stress and limited cooling
  • Thermal Refugia: Low heat stress and strong cooling
  • Stress Buffered Systems: High heat stress but strong cooling

Results

Extreme High Heat Years

Extreme high heat years were 2016 and 2020 for Tingles Island (Figure 2).

Figure 2. Mean yearly HDH for each site at ASIS. Extreme high heat years (red points) are years when mean HDH exceeded the site-specific 90th percentile value (red dashed line).

Extreme Low Cooling Years

Extreme low cooling years were 2011 and 2018 for Tingles Island (Figure 3).

Figure 3. Mean yearly CDH for each site at ASIS. Extreme low cooling years (blue points) are years when mean CDH exceeded the site-specific 90th percentile value (blue dashed line).

Compound Stress Years

There were no compound stress years at any of the sites at ASIS (Figure 4).

Figure 4. Compound stress years (purple points) are years when mean CDH and mean HDH exceeded the site-specific 90th percentile values.

How does ASIS compare across the region?

Figure 5. Heat event structure across three coastal National Park Service units (CACO, ASIS, FIIS). Each point represents a site-level average of the mean number of warming events per year (frequency) and the mean percentage of time above the thermal threshold (duration). Dashed lines divide the figure into four interpretive thermal regimes. Labels show the average number of monitoring years contributing to each site-level estimate.

Across the three coastal NCBN parks, clear regional patterns emerge. At CACO, most sites fall in the category of having fewer and shorter heat‑stress events. An exception is the partially restored East Harbor system, which shows a different pattern. Overall, CACO sites tend to experience heat stress as brief or infrequent pulses rather than long, sustained events.

In contrast, Tingles Island at ASIS experiences heat stress much more often, and these events add up throughout the season. This pattern is expected for parks located in warmer parts of the region, where longer and more frequent heat events are common.

FIIS sites fall between these two extremes. Heat‑stress conditions vary widely across the park, depending on where each site is located. For example, Moriches Bay shows short, frequent warming events, while Great South Bay experiences longer or more sustained heat episodes. This mix reflects the diversity of habitats and local conditions across Fire Island.

These results show that sites across the regional scale experience different heat stress conditions and even sites within the same park respond in different ways. This raises an important questions that will require further data collection and analysis: how are some of the most chronically stressed sites, like Moriches Bay, Pleasant Bay, and Tingles Island still able to support eelgrass populations?

What are the impacts of cooling?

Now that we’ve seen sites experience heat stress differently, we can look at cooling relief from heat events. Here, we divide the eelgrass into the four previously described cooling regimes based on the balance between thermal stress and thermal relief:

Figure 6. Thermal stress and cooling recovery across three coastal National Park Service units (CACO, ASIS, FIIS). Each point represents a site‑level average of the mean heating degree hours per day (thermal stress) and the mean cooling degree hours per day (thermal recovery). Dashed lines divide the figure into four interpretive recovery regimes. Labels show the average number of monitoring years contributing to each site‑level estimate.

The balance between heat stress events and cooling recovery also varies across the region and within parks. Pleasant Bay and Moriches Bay receive some of the strongest cooling periods among the chronically warm sites, second only to the fully open tidal systems on Cape Cod. This pattern reflects their position relative to inlets where tidal flushing brings in cooler ocean water that helps moderate warmer temperatures and sustain populations of eelgrass. In contrast, sites with more limited flushing, like Great South Bay and East Harbor, show weaker cooling relief consistent with restricted or partially restored flow. These sites match site conditions that no longer support eelgrass. Tingles Island falls between these two outcomes as it receives little cooling, sits between a stable and thermal refugia zone, and supports sparse eelgrass populations.

Key Takeaways

ASIS Key Takeaways

Across NCBN parks, Tingles Island stands out as one of the most heat-stressed locations due to frequent and prolonged heat events that accumulate throughout the season. This thermal pattern is expected given its southern latitude relative to FIIS (NY) and CACO (MA). The Tingles Island transect supports only sparse eelgrass populations, reflecting moderate cooling, but still challenging environment compared to denser sites like Pleasant Bay and Moriches Bay.

While this analysis focuses on thermal conditions alone, other water quality factors like dissolved oxygen, turbidity, salinity, and pH also play a key role in shaping eelgrass health. At Tingles Island, long- term trend reports show significant declines in eelgrass conditions (canopy height, biomass, and percent cover, shoot density, and biomass ratios), trends driven by a combination of chronically poor water quality and heat stress (Nagel et al. 2025a). Together these observations point to ecological pressure on the system.

In parallel with these environmental assessments, NPS scientists and partners are using genomics to better understand why some eelgrass populations can withstand warming while other decline. By sequencing plants from Maine to North Carolina, we can identify genetic differences linked to heat tolerance and local adaptation. These results will guide future restoration planning and identify donor populations for transplanting seeds to help vulnerable meadows keep pace with rising sea temperatures.

🟦 Network‑Wide Key Takeaways

• Across NCBN coastal parks, eelgrass beds experience a wide range of thermal conditions, from sites with prolonged, cumulative heat exposure to sites with strong cooling capacity.

• Understanding both heating intensity and cooling relief provides essential context for interpreting long‑term eelgrass trends, genomic thermal tolerance, and vulnerability to climate‑driven change.

• Applying thermal metrics alongside genomic data will help identify populations with potential heat tolerance and strengthen site‑selection models for restoration and transplanting.

• Integrating eelgrass distribution from long‑term transects with temperature patterns will help parks diagnose change, identify drivers of decline, and prioritize management actions.

These thermal metrics are part of an ongoing collaborative project and represent a novel approach to characterizing eelgrass stress across NCBN parks. Thresholds linking these metrics to genomic patterns and adaptive capacity are still being refined in coordination with project cooperators. Readers can learn more about the broader genomics effort, restoration framework, and supporting documentation on the Resilient Eelgrass Project Sharepoint.
